accessAttack: Route: a 30-second scrollback read. tmux capture-pane -p -t %N | tail -40, or just looking at the pane you already have open. Crude thrash announces itself as co-located repetition in text (same tool call, same failing test, same file rewritten) and humans spot repetition in adjacent text instantly. That is fatal to 88, which claims effectively unobtainable, and it is the same route that kills C5. The author note is also self-refuting: all of it already sits in transcripts Cargento reads means the evidence is on disk and on screen. What survives the attack is the non-crude case: for a slow wedge, 30 seconds of looking returns a confident FALSE NEGATIVE, because output is moving so the user concludes working. Discriminating that needs the same content compared across intervals, which is the correlate-across-time band. Lands at 68, not 88.
impactAttack: 93 smuggles in the word reliably, and reliably is what a repeated-tool-call heuristic cannot be. The detector must fire on legitimate iteration: TDD red-green, flaky-test diagnosis, a lint fix loop, a long build retried. Two false alarms and the user goes back to checking panes, which is the behaviour it was built to replace. The loss is also compute and quota rather than work, and it is bounded by the next glance, which a 3-to-12-session user takes often. The actual walk-away behaviour change belongs to D4 and H2 delivery, not to detection: knowing a session is stuck while you sit at the desk changes 10 minutes of your day, not your working pattern. 78, not 93.

accessAttack: The author concedes the whole attack in the needs field: composable from data already on screen. Today route: sweep the panes, and if none is showing a prompt, leave. Developers already run this informal all-clear constantly, and it is the reason the walk-away habit exists at all. The user also does not need N minutes: the away-duration is set by the errand, not by the agents, so the horizon is decoration on a binary decision. For the paranoid there is a scripted route a competent dev writes in ten minutes: tmux list-panes -a -F, capture-pane each, grep for a prompt marker. 85 is scoring the cost of the COMPOSITION, which is Cargento build cost, not the cost of the inputs.
impactAttack: Compulsive checking is not an information deficit. It is a trust problem plus a near-zero cost of checking: alt-tab is free, so a 90-percent-accurate all-clear becomes a SECOND thing to check rather than a replacement for the first. The author admits the item is only honest once C2 exists, which means its impact is borrowed from an unbuilt detector and should not be banked now. Worse, it is redundant against its own neighbours: if D4 and H2 deliver, being reachable subsumes being told you are free, and a user who can be pinged does not need permission to leave. If they do not deliver, D5 is the promise that breaks trust the first time it is wrong, which the author also wrote down and then scored 82 anyway.

accessAttack: Weakest of my nine access attacks: quantified attention-spend genuinely is cross-session and cross-time, so the axis logic holds and this half mostly survives. The deductions are two. First, a scriptable route exists over data the user owns: timestamps of user turns in the transcript files under the Claude projects directory, one awk away for a competent dev, though a normal user will not write it. Second, the ADEQUATE approximation is free and already possessed, because the user lived the week and knows perfectly well whether it went on answering agents. 85 asserts effectively unobtainable; scriptable-plus-already-felt puts it at the top of the correlate-across-time band instead. 74.
impactAttack: This is G4 (History, streaks, sessions this week) with a delegation justification bolted on, and the same author scored G4 at impact 14. Nothing follows from the number: the user who resents interruptions already resents them, and every action the item gestures at is separately scored as F1 and F2. The tell is in the note itself, the one artifact here a user would voluntarily show their manager, which is an org-politics deliverable, not a change in what the user does at the keyboard. The reporting cadence is also wrong for the impact band: a weekly retrospective drives a setup change monthly at best, which is not a real decision on a regular basis. Interesting, mild action follows: 50.

accessAttack: Both readings come in low. As INFORMATION: this item exists because a user wrote it on a sticky, which is direct proof the user already had the observation. Irritation is a perfectly good five-times detector, and answering the same question repeatedly is the most salient experience in the whole set. As an ACTION, which is what the second half of the item actually is: the fix is one command a competent user already knows, /permissions in Claude Code, an allow entry in settings.json, or a single skill file, and the harness offers to persist the decision in-place at the moment of the prompt. Neither reading requires visiting several places or manual correlation, so 80 is unsupportable in either direction. 40.
impactAttack: The blocker is not knowing you should; it is activation energy plus a rational reluctance to grant a standing permission you may regret. A dashboard card counting to five reduces neither. It also competes with a strictly better-placed intervention that already ships: the in-prompt do-not-ask-again offer arrives at the moment of the decision, with full context, when the user is already stopped. A retrospective nudge arrives when the user is doing something else and will be dismissed. And where the repeated question is a genuine judgement call, the user is declining to automate it deliberately, so the count is not evidence of a defect. 50.

accessAttack: The note refutes the score in its own words: Spacedock state files already say where everything is, and half the item already ships as the stage strip. So for the only population that HAS stages, the stage is one cat of a state file or one FO status call away, in a place they know to look. The remaining half, the tripwire, is an ACTION not information, and the today-route is a three-line shell loop over that state file into osascript display notification, or a single grep run when you check anyway. Outside Spacedock the intended stage does not exist as data at all, so there is no access for Cargento to create either. 80 is measuring where the user has to declare the line, which is a UI gap, not an access gap. 45.
impactAttack: A tripwire changes WHEN you look, not what you decide, and at a stage boundary the workflow gate already blocks and waits, so nothing is lost by looking late. Because the strips shipped, the incremental impact is the tripwire alone, and it must be measured against the existing approval gate that already interrupts the user. The addressable population is Spacedock workflow users, a narrow slice of a nine-harness product, which caps the on-a-regular-basis clause hard. It also inherits a configuration burden the author admits has no home yet, and features requiring the user to pre-declare a condition are chronically unconfigured. 55.

accessAttack: git status and git diff --stat in the session worktree name every file the agent touched: one command, in the place the user already looks, and touching files outside the intended area IS the operational definition of drift. Inside Spacedock the intended scope is declared and cheap to read, which the author concedes with free in Spacedock. Outside it the rails are implicit, which means the comparison does not exist for Cargento either, so 85 is the textbook circular case: rated near-unobtainable because nobody has built an inference that may not be buildable. Nonexistent is not inaccessible. 45.
impactAttack: Scope inference has an unfixable precision problem: legitimate work constantly touches an adjacent test, type, import, fixture or config, so a detector that cries drift on those is muted within a week, and a muted detector changes no behaviour. The real gate already exists downstream and costs nothing: the user reads the diff before committing, with perfect precision and zero false positives. Catching drift twenty minutes earlier saves agent compute, not user hours, and the impact scale measures the user. The failure mode this claims to prevent, an agent quietly rewriting the wrong subsystem, is also caught for free by E4-style dirty-worktree review at the same moment. 48.

accessAttack: This is the most eyeball-detectable failure mode on the entire board. The same test failing five times in a row, or consecutive failed tool calls, appears as co-located repetition in the last 30 lines of the pane, and tmux capture-pane -p -t %N | tail -30 retrieves it for a pane you are not watching. Human pattern matching on repeated adjacent text is close to instant, and no memory or cross-time correlation is required because the repeats are on screen together. 78 is not defensible for a signal a user reads in five seconds once looking. The residual value is doing it across twelve sessions unprompted and while the user is absent, but that is D4/H2 delivery, not access to the fact. 50.
impactAttack: My weakest impact attack of the nine, and I concede most of it: a loop eating a five-hour window is concrete loss and the corrective action is obvious and immediate. Two deductions only. The loss is bounded by the next glance, and a user with 3-12 live sessions glances often, so the catastrophic version needs an hours-long unattended window that is a minority of sessions. And the wasted-quota framing assumes the window would otherwise have gone to useful work, which for a user sitting at the desk with the other eleven sessions already running it usually would not. 68, a mild trim rather than a kill; the item falls out of the quadrant on access, not on impact.

accessAttack: Every input is already on screen for the modelled user. /usage reports percent used AND reset time, and Barista pins both to the status line permanently, so the user sees them without asking. The projection is one division, and users already speak the coarse version out loud: I am at 80 percent with two hours left in the window. Two /usage readings twenty minutes apart give a MEASURED rate well inside thirty seconds of deliberate effort. This is the synthesis pattern in its purest form on this board: a ratio over two continuously visible numbers, scored as though the ratio were a fact the user cannot reach. The author caught himself doing exactly this on A4 and did not propagate the correction here. 50.
impactAttack: Compare the action set at 80 percent used against the action set at 22 minutes to the wall: identical. Stop starting big jobs, take a handoff summary, switch harness. The extra precision improves the TIMING of an action the coarse signal already triggers, which is convenience, not prevented loss. Burn rate over a bursty agent workload is also a poor predictor of the next hour, so the projection will be visibly wrong often enough to send the user back to the coarse heuristic, and a projection people stop believing changes nothing. Its ceiling depends on A1, whose data arrives from an authenticated API and needs a security-promise amendment the product has not agreed to pay, so its impact is contingent on an unbought dependency. 62.

accessAttack: The min is taken over ETAs that no harness produces, which the briefing states flatly. That means the number does not EXIST anywhere, rather than being hard to reach: you cannot be denied access to an estimate nobody has computed, and the barrier is accuracy, not access. Score the underlying user question instead, will anything want me in the next fifteen minutes, and the today-route is a timer: sleep 900 and a beep, or a pomodoro, which is exactly what people already do. Add the free heuristic that a session which just began a large task will not want you soon. The author names the mechanism in the needs field, the minimum over ETAs Cargento already computes, which prices Cargento build cost and not user effort. 52.
impactAttack: Nobody organises a break around a clock time handed to them by a dashboard; they leave for as long as the errand takes and come back when they come back. If the ETA is wrong, and turn-duration estimation is bad enough that no harness attempts it, the user either returns to nothing finished or leaves a gate sitting idle for ten minutes, which is worse than never having been told. It also competes head-on with being notified, and notification strictly dominates: do not remember a time, get pinged. If D4 and H2 work, D6 is redundant; if they do not, D6 is unreliable. Either way the walking-away behaviour does not change. 52.
